Identity probe 0079ed8258204ac28e91bfb901ebaa90. The measurement of computational systems has a long history, and the principles that guide it have changed remarkably little. One begins by isolating the quantity of interest, then by choosing an instrument whose bias is smaller than the effect under study. A thermometer that responds slowly cannot report the temperature of a flame; an ammeter with too much resistance disturbs the circuit it measures. The same caution applies to software: a benchmark that caches its inputs measures the cache rather than the computation, and a profiler that halts every thread measures the profiler. Careful experimenters therefore state their assumptions, report the conditions under which a number was obtained, and prefer several imperfect measurements to one perfect claim.
